newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Italy government allies disagree over budget.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Italy government allies disagree over budget.

text.p: Parties supporting Italy's government failed to reach an agreement on Monday over the 1997 budget after the hard left spurned Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi's call for a tougher package.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi, whose centre-left administration is expected to unveil the budget later this week, met his key political allies to try to iron out problems over proposed cuts in health and pension spending.
"We made some progress but a few points of disagreement remain," a statement from Prodi's office said after the meeting.
"We will work to overcome them with the aim of guaranteeing Italy's entry into European monetary union as well as social equality," it added.

Ciampi, worried that Italy is falling behind in its bid to join the first wave of countries into the single European currency planned for 1999, has demanded that the budget should tackle some areas of sensitive welfare spending.

His call was backed by Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio, who hinted at the weekend that a tough budget might be rewarded with an interest rate cut, but has run into serious flak from the hard-left Communist Refoundation party.
Without Refoundation's support the government cannot control a majority in the lower house of parliament where the budget has to be ratified by the end of the year.

Ciampi has already announced that the package will cut 32.4 trillion lire ($21.2 billion) off next year's deficit, but analysts are sceptical that this target can be hit without action on the generous welfare state.
"Wall Street might want pensions to be cut, but Wall Street is not in the (Italian) government," Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti told reporters.
Government officials said party leaders would meet later in the week to discuss the problem.

"It is pointless trying to deny it, there are disagreements. We are carrying on talking even if I don't think we'll be able to strike a deal by the end of today," Gerardo Bianchi, leader of the centrist Popular Party, said after Monday's meeting.

Bianchi suggested the government should introduce a special "Maastricht Tax" to help Italy meet demanding criteria imposed by the Maastricht Treaty for countries wishing to join European Monetary and Economic Union (EMU) from the outset.
At present Italy fails to meet any of the criteria and a weak budget would further hinder its progess towards EMU.

Newspapers reported on Monday that the Treasury was considering introducing another mini-budget before the end of the year, in addition to the official 1997 budget, to try make even bigger in-roads into the state deficit.
The government has already approved one mini-budget this year as accounts weakened in the face of a slowing economy.
Under Maastricht, EMU founder members have to cut the ratio between their annual budget deficit and gross domestic product to no more than three percent by the end of 1997.
Italy is forecasting a deficit/GDP ratio of 6.09 percent this year and 4.52 percent next.

"Italy will make strong, substantial progress in getting closer to the 3.0 percent target set by the Maastricht Treaty" Ciampi told reporters at the weekend. First he has to persuade the hard left that the budget pain is worth it.
